articles.title: Elon Musk's message to Cursor's 1,000-plus engineers after the $60 billion takeover: We are behind, and the company beating us is...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Elon Musk waited until the ink was dry to tell Cursor what he actually wanted from it. On the day SpaceX confirmed it had completed its $60 billion ac.
articles.body: Elon Musk waited until the ink was dry to tell Cursor what he actually wanted from it. On the day SpaceX confirmed it had completed its $60 billion acquisition of the AI coding startup, Musk dialled into an all-hands video call and told more than 1,000 Cursor employees that SpaceX's AI division had slipped behind its rivals, according to a report in The Information citing five people with knowledge of the meeting.His framing was blunt. Tesla and SpaceX lead their markets, he said, but Grok does not, and he is not used to losing. The fix, as he put it to staff gathered at Cursor's San Francisco headquarters and at smaller offices, is for them to help SpaceXAI catch up quickly. He also told the room that AI models will eventually become too advanced for humans to control, which is exactly why he wants his side building them first.Elon Musk says Grok is losing the AI race to AnthropicThe praise for a competitor was the most revealing part of the call. Musk said Anthropic was leading the AI race and was a strong rival, one person told The Information. That is an awkward thing to concede when earlier reporting suggested xAI's own engineers reached for Claude when they wanted to code.His counterweight is hardware. Musk said SpaceX would keep stockpiling more compute than anyone else in the race, an argument Cursor made publicly too when it said the deal gives it "access to the largest fleet of GPUs in the world."Cursor CEO Michael Truell now reports directly to Elon Musk at SpaceXAIThe acquisition was structured unusually from the start. SpaceX signed a tech-sharing and compute deal with Cursor in April that carried an option to buy the company for $60 billion, exercised it in June days after its own IPO, and closed it in mid-August. Leadership had told staff early on that little would change day to day.The org chart says otherwise. Cursor CEO Michael Truell now holds a leadership role at SpaceXAI and reports directly to Musk, co-founder Aman Sanger has moved into pretraining, and Sualeh Asif is director of machine learning. Slack workspaces have been merged, staff are being nudged towards the Palo Alto offices, and Truell has offered to buy them copies of Liftoff, a book on SpaceX's early years.Cursor hit $4 billion in revenue, but 45 staff have quit since AprilCursor is not a distressed asset. It reportedly crossed $4 billion in annualised revenue in June, and headcount has more than quadrupled over the past year on the back of heavy sales hiring. But 45 people, mostly from product and engineering, have left since April, The Information reports, including roughly 20 who arrived through the Graphite acquisition. Recent senior exits cover reinforcement learning, design, brand, enterprise sales and the general counsel's office.The gap Musk described on that call has not been closed by the deal, only funded. SpaceX now owns the coding tool developers reach for, alongside a model most of them do not. Whether Grok narrows that distance is a question for the next twelve months. SpaceXAI and Cursor did not respond to requests for comment.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: 15 grados de desigualdad, la brecha térmica que separa al lujo de las favelas brasileñas
articles.summary: Ailén Desirée Montes
articles.body:
São Paulo, 25 ago (EFE).- En 2020, vecinos de Morumbi, uno de los barrios más ricos de São Paulo, pidieron a la Alcaldía erigir un muro de tres metros de altura para aislar un parque público que se estaba construyendo en el límite con Paraisópolis, la segunda favela más grande de la ciudad.

La pared de concreto finalmente fue rechazada, pero imágenes de satélite revelan que entre ambos barrios ya existe un muro invisible, pero sofocante: una frontera de 15 grados de temperatura.

Mientras en las calles arboladas de Morumbi la temperatura de una tarde de verano ronda los 30 °C, basta con cruzar una avenida para ingresar a esta favela, con más de 58.000 habitantes, y descubrir que la superficie puede alcanzar hasta 45 °C.

Esta disparidad no es casual. Una investigación del Centro de Estudios de la Favela (Cefavela) evidencia que en las 1,359 favelas paulistas, donde viven 1.72 millones de personas en solo el 4 % del territorio urbano, la temperatura media de superficie supera habitualmente los 40 °C.

Victor Nascimento, uno de los investigadores de este estudio, explica a EFE que las viviendas hacinadas de hormigón, los techos de fibrocemento o metal y la falta de ventanas para la ventilación cruzada convierten las casas en "hornos".

Señala que combatir el calor se vuelve aún más difícil por la falta de servicios básicos de agua y electricidad en muchas viviendas, en las que a menudo se recurre a conexiones clandestinas, lo que imposibilita que los habitantes usen ventiladores o incluso tomen duchas para refrescarse.

Esta precariedad habitacional se suma a los problemas de la planificación urbana. Según el Observatorio del Clima, muchas ciudades toman decisiones "a contramano de la adaptación climática".

La falta de inversión en drenaje pluvial, saneamiento ambiental integral y estructuras sostenibles en las periferias convierte en frágil la gestión de riesgos y deja desprotegidas a las comunidades ante inundaciones, deslaves u olas de calor.

Para la secretaria ejecutiva de la Red de Adaptación Antirracista, Thaynah Gutierrez, el calor extremo en las favelas "profundiza las desigualdades del racismo ambiental".

Precisa que la ciudad sufre una separación entre lo que los investigadores denominan "zonas de sacrificio" en la periferia, desprovistas de árboles e infraestructura básica, mientras que los barrios de mayor nivel socioeconómico disfrutan de equilibrio térmico y vegetación.

"El hecho de que se haya permitido que las periferias se construyeran únicamente con concreto, con lo que los habitantes tenían a mano para construir sus viviendas, hizo que estos espacios resultaran muy inadecuados en el contexto de la crisis climática que estamos enfrentando", dice la especialista.

Para Gutierrez, no es viable "seguir con la narrativa" de que ""a gente ni siquiera debería haber ocupado esos territorios".

"Después de 40 años de ocupación, ya es demasiado tarde para decir que la gente no debería vivir ahí. Ahora es responsabilidad de las autoridades públicas reconocer el error y apoyar que estas viviendas sean más resilientes", opina.

Por ello, organizaciones sociales exigen reformas estructurales e inversiones prioritarias en los territorios vulnerables.

Una de las principales demandas es la aplicación de la ley de 2008 de Asistencia Técnica para Viviendas de Interés Social, que garantiza a las familias de bajos ingresos en Brasil el derecho a asistencia técnica gratuita de arquitectos e ingenieros para proyectar, construir, reformar o regularizar viviendas de interés social.

Esto, entre otras cuestiones, permitiría planificar la reforma de viviendas con ventanas colocadas estratégicamente, techos verdes y aislamiento térmico, además de incorporar límites térmicos obligatorios en nuevos proyectos habitacionales.

Los desafíos climáticos de las periferias se discutirán en la cuarta edición del Foro Latinoamericano de Economía Verde (FLEV), que organiza la Agencia EFE en São Paulo el próximo 3 de septiembre y que contará con la participación de autoridades, expertos y representantes de empresas y organismos multilaterales.

El evento cuenta con el patrocinio de WWF-Brasil y ApexBrasil, así como con el apoyo de AYA Earth Partners, Imaflora y Observatorio del Clima.

articles.title: Vietnam Revises EPR Policy to Improve Circularity
articles.summary: The Vietnam Department of Environment’s draft policy calls for strengthening the role of private sector stakeholders in implementing EPR practices.
articles.body:
Vietnam is making moves to revise its extended producer responsibility (EPR) policy to better promote the development of a circular economy.

Announced at the "Pathways for a Robust Extended Producer Responsibility System in Vietnam " workshop in Hanoi, the revision applies to the 2020 Law on Environmental Protection and its included regulations, including provisions addressing EPR.

Mills Update: Japan, Vietnam and Indonesia Producers on How Sustainability is Evolving

Op-Ed: Doubling Down on Circular Fashion Requires More Than Regulation

Vietnam Faces Trade Squeeze as Wages Rise

Tăng The Cuong, director general of Vietnam's Department of Environment, said that EPR should not be viewed merely as a financial obligation for businesses, but rather a mechanism that incentivizes changes in product design, material selection, collection and recycling systems, and investment in circular solutions.

Cuong said that Vietnam has made significant progress in establishing and implementing EPR over the past six years, but the practice still has room for improvement. To boost transparency and effectiveness, the nation needs to offer stronger incentives for the collection and recycling market.

The Vietnam Department of Environment's draft policy calls for strengthening the role of private sector stakeholders in implementing EPR practices. The nation aims to do that by focusing on developing policies, legal frameworks and monitoring mechanisms that would require producers to directly organize collection and recycling of post-consumer products and packaging either independently or using third-party producer responsibility organization recyclers. The updated policy also will eliminate the ability for producers to simply make financial contributions to the Vietnam Environment Protection Fund as a means of fulfilling their recycling obligations.

Francesca Nardini, deputy resident representative of the United Nations Development Program in Vietnam said the next challenge for the nation will be developing an EPR system that operates effectively, sustainably and in accordance with market demands.

"EPR should not only ensure regulatory compliance or meet recycling targets, but also help transform how resources circulate within the economy, create value from materials that might otherwise become waste and encourage investment and innovation," she said.

Apparel is one of Vietnam's largest industries, valued at $7.52 billion in 2025 and growing at a compound annual growth rate of 6.80 percent to reach $11.14 billion by 2031, according to Ken Research. The country's packaging sector is heavily connected to apparel, particularly with the growth of e-commerce.

During the event in Hanoi, Dr. Fritz Flanderka, executive director of packaging specialist the Reclay Group, said there is no universal EPR model that will fit all scenarios. The core focus can be shifting recycling and collection responsibility to businesses, but the design and operation of these systems must be tailored to the markets and institutions they regulate.

With that in mind, PROs will play a central role in any EPR policy, connecting producers with collection, sorting and recycling networks. Experts at the Hanoi summit said the responsibilities of PROs, along with capacity requirements and oversight mechanisms, must be clearly defined in EPR policy. Under the policy revisions currently under consideration, PROs would be mandated to meet requirements related to organizational ability for collection, financial capacity, electronic data management and accounting.

Currently, informal waste pickers and scrap collectors make up a large portion of Vietnam's collection system, so the new policy also will factor in that labor so that workers aren't left behind. And the revision also will take into account the time constraints and investments needed to roll out a more developed EPR system, so mandatory recycling rates would be adjusted in phases to allow producers time to prepare for compliance.

Francesca Nardini, deputy resident representative of the United Nations Development Program in Vietnam said the next challenge for the nation will be developing an EPR system that operates effectively, sustainably and in accordance with market demands.

"EPR should not only ensure regulatory compliance or meet recycling targets, but also help transform how resources circulate within the economy, create value from materials that might otherwise become waste and encourage investment and innovation," she said.

Apparel is one of Vietnam's largest industries, valued at $7.52 billion in 2025 and growing at a compound annual growth rate of 6.80 percent to reach $11.14 billion by 2031, according to Ken Research. The country's packaging sector is heavily connected to apparel, particularly with the growth of e-commerce.

During the event in Hanoi, Dr. Fritz Flanderka, executive director of packaging specialist the Reclay Group, said there is no universal EPR model that will fit all scenarios. The core focus can be shifting recycling and collection responsibility to businesses, but the design and operation of these systems must be tailored to the markets and institutions they regulate.

With that in mind, PROs will play a central role in any EPR policy, connecting producers with collection, sorting and recycling networks. Experts at the Hanoi summit said the responsibilities of PROs, along with capacity requirements and oversight mechanisms, must be clearly defined in EPR policy. Under the policy revisions currently under consideration, PROs would be mandated to meet requirements related to organizational ability for collection, financial capacity, electronic data management and accounting.

Currently, informal waste pickers and scrap collectors make up a large portion of Vietnam's collection system, so the new policy also will factor in that labor so that workers aren't left behind. And the revision also will take into account the time constraints and investments needed to roll out a more developed EPR system, so mandatory recycling rates would be adjusted in phases to allow producers time to prepare for compliance.

articles.title: What is CTE, and how many former NFL players have been diagnosed with it?
articles.summary: So far, the degenerative brain disease has only been diagnosed after a person's death.
articles.body:
Editor's Note: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org .

(NEXSTAR) – A new study led by researchers out of Massachusetts suggests that among those who have played in the NFL, at least one in four may develop chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a disease that carries no cure and has only been diagnosed after death.

The study , published in The BMJ, reviewed the hundreds of NFL players who died between 2008 and 2021. Of the more than 1,700 who died, researchers reported that the brains of 338 were studied. Postmortem brain analysis has, so far, been the only proven method of determining whether someone has CTE, a degenerative brain disease.

Of the 338 brains that were studied, it was determined that 315 donors had a CTE diagnosis.

Among players who died within the last six years – a time in which "brain donation was more frequent" – researchers said 235 NFL players donated their brains for analysis. More than 210 were found to have CTE.

Just over 200 of the 338 whose brains were analyzed had been previously diagnosed with dementia. The study found that donors with dementia were later found to have more severe cases of CTE: 94 had Stage 4 CTE, considered the most severe level.

Broadly speaking, CTE impacts how the brain functions. Research has suggested that CTE is "linked to a build-up of abnormal proteins that damage brain tissue and cause brain cells to undergo cell death," the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention explains .

CTE is often found in people who have experienced repeated impacts to the head, making football players among the most commonly associated with the disease. However, as the Boston University CTE Center notes , the condition has been linked to boxers and soccer and hockey players, as well as those who have served in the military or as first responders. Even athletes who stopped participating in sports in high school and college have been diagnosed with CTE.

Symptoms can take years or decades to develop, experts say. When they do appear, they can last for months or years. The exact symptoms associated with CTE are unclear, but the CDC explains that those who are diagnosed are later described as having "problems with thinking, emotions, mood, suicidal thoughts and/or behaviors that became serious enough to get in the way of normal daily activities."

"However, having these symptoms does not necessarily mean a person has CTE," the CDC adds. "It is important to talk to a doctor if you, a family member, or friend have any questions or concerns. Treatments are available to help with many of these symptoms."

Research to better understand CTE – including how it develops, what risk factors may be associated with it, and how to diagnose it earlier – continues, according to Boston University.

Hundreds of NFL players diagnosed with CTE after death

As the latest study found, there have been hundreds of NFL players who, after their brains were studied following their deaths, were diagnosed with CTE. (A 2023 report said that of the 376 former NFL players studied by Boston University's CTE Center, 345 had been diagnosed with the brain disease.)

Among the most recently diagnosed was former Dallas Cowboys defensive end Marshawn Kneeland , who died by suicide in November following a high-speed chase with police. Boston University researchers analyzed Kneeland's brain tissue and determined he had Stage 1 CTE.

Aaron Hernandez , whose 2017 death was ruled a suicide, was found to have Stage 3 CTE. He had been in prison at the time of his death in a murder case.

Former Tennessee Titan Frank Wycheck , who died in 2023 after apparently hitting his head in a fall at home, had Stage 3 CTE, his family said. Former NFL Pro Bowl wide receiver Demaryius Thomas had been dealing with depression, anxiety and other CTE symptoms at the time of his 2021 death. His family later confirmed he had Stage 2 CTE.

Irv Cross , a former NFL player turned CBS anchor, was found to have had CTE following his 2021 death. His widow, Liz Cross, told the Associated Press in 2023 that the former Philadelphia Eagles cornerback had experienced depression, mood swings and memory loss that made him not "want to be with people." Boston University researchers determined Cross had Stage 4 CTE .

Phillip Adams , who spent several seasons in the NFL, fatally shot six people in Rock Hill, South Carolina, before killing himself in 2021. An autopsy later showed he had Stage 2 CTE , Nexstar's WJZY reported.

Shane Tamura, the man who killed four people in the same New York City building that houses the NFL's headquarters, was found to have CTE . In a note found on his body, Tamura expressed a grievance with the league – he played football, but never in the NFL – and claimed he suffered from CTE.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Avulux lands FDA de novo classification for light-sensitive migraine lenses
articles.summary: Avulux’s lens technology uses a optical filters to block up to 97% of blue, amber, and red light while letting soothing green light through.
articles.body:
Avulux has obtained de novo marketing authorisation from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its optical lenses for managing light sensitivity associated with migraine, making it the first product of its kind to achieve the designation.

The Florida-based company's precision optical filter is indicated to decrease the impact of light sensitivity in patients aged 12 years and older diagnosed with episodic migraine.

Research indicates that over 45 million people in the US are affected by episodic migraine, while up to 90% of people living with the neurological condition cite light sensitivity as a symptom, with up to 60% of migraine attacks triggered by harsh light or glare. Episodic migraine occurs on fewer than 15 days per month.

Worn like regular eyeglasses, Avulux's lens technology uses a dual-band optical filter that is designed to block up to 97% of blue, amber, and red light -- light wavelengths that stimulate intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (IPRGCs) and have been demonstrated to exacerbate headache-associated light sensitivity -- while letting soothing green light pass through, the company stated.

Clearance for the eyeglasses, which are intended to complement rather than replace usual migraine care such as the gold standard of triptans, was supported by Avulux's clinical evidence from several studies. In a clinical evaluation (NCT04341298), Avulux's IPRGC lenses were associated with clinically and statistically significant reductions in two- and four-hour headache pain in a post-hoc analyses of 78 patients with baseline headache pain scores ≥ 2 on an 11-point scale.

Avulux's CEO, Dr Charles Posternack, commented: "For a long time, light sensitivity was seen as just a symptom of migraine. That thinking has changed. There is growing recognition that light sensitivity is a serious medical concern in its own right.

"This authorisation gives patients and providers a clear, FDA-recognised option designed specifically to manage the impact of light in those with migraine, one we hope will soon become the standard of medical care in this population."

In the medtech industry, companies are at various developmental stages for migraine treatments that are designed to provide relief via neuromodulation. These include ShiraTronics, which is developing an implantable neuromodulation system for chronic migraine (CM) relief. In a readout from September 2025 , the company's system demonstrated an 11.3-day mean reduction in monthly headache days (MHD) for CM patients in a pilot study evaluating its device.

Meanwhile, Theranica 's neuromodulation-based therapy for relieving migraine symptoms secured FDA clearance in March 2023, and Nocira gained approval breakthrough device designation from the agency in April 2022 for its automated variable pulse insufflation (AVPI) device that administers gentle, controlled puffs of air in the ears to treat migraine attacks. However, prescription drugs such as triptans remain the go-to treatment for the condition.

"Avulux lands FDA de novo classification for light-sensitive migraine lenses" was originally created and published by Medical Device Network , a GlobalData owned brand.

articles.title: The U.S. just recorded its first two deaths from measles for 2026
articles.summary: Two people who were not vaccinated against measles died of the disease in Pennsylvania, public health officials said on Tuesday—these are the first measles f...
articles.body:
Two people who were not vaccinated against measles died of the disease in Pennsylvania, public health officials said on Tuesday—these are the first measles fatalities in the state in 35 years. The deaths have come as the number of measles cases across the U.S. has exploded, with 36 outbreaks recorded so far this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Both people were residents of Lancaster County. State health officials said no other details would be released to protect the privacy of the victims and their families.

So far, 2026 has seen 2,777 confirmed cases of measles, an increase from 2,289 cases for the whole of 2025, according to the CDC. This year the Pennsylvania Department of Health has reported 393 cases so far; last year Pennsylvania reported just 16 infections.

Measles is a preventable disease; the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine effectively protects against infections—in fact, it has done such a good job of lowering measles incidence that, in 2000, the U.S. was declared to have eliminated the disease entirely. Now, as vaccine rates drop as a result of increased skepticism toward the shots, infections are back on the rise, and public health experts expect the nation will soon lose its elimination status.

That matters for public health: Measles is the most contagious human virus we know of. It has a fatality rate of one to three deaths per 1,000 cases in the U.S. And it can cause severe health issues, including pneumonia and brain swelling. Some 20 percent of people who contract the disease require hospitalization. Children and pregnant women are among the most at risk of severe disease; measles can also harm unborn fetuses.

Pennsylvania's secretary of health Debra Bogen encouraged residents to get vaccinated against the disease in a statement . Nationwide, inoculations have been declining: New data from the CDC show the proportion of kindergarteners who received the MMR vaccine has fallen from 95 percent to 92.4 percent over the past decade.

"Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don't fully understand the potential severity of the illness," Bogen said. "We want to ensure every Pennsylvanian has the information they need to protect themselves, their loved ones and their communities. As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand that the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles."

The two deaths from measles were confirmed just weeks after President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at altering the childhood vaccine schedule, particularly by splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate shots. When announcing the order, Trump falsely claimed the MMR vaccine can be "lethal." Members of his own administration made efforts to walk the pronouncement back: In an interview on Sunday , Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services administrator Mehmet Oz said the MMR shot is not, in fact, "a lethal vaccine." The overwhelming evidence shows the MMR vaccine is safe and effective, with a very low risk of serious side effects.

articles.title: Startups are selling states on cloud seeding.
articles.summary:
States struggling with dwindling water resources as a result of climate change are turning to a new generation of companies claiming they can induce rain or snowfall. Rainmaker, a cloud seeding company based in El Segundo, California, says it has helped generate at least 143 million gallons of water for Oregon and Utah.

articles.title: How the Crown-of-Thorns Starfish Liquefies Living Coral
articles.summary: When a crown-of-thorns starfish settles onto a coral reef, it turns its own stomach inside out and gets to work dissolving living coral from the inside. Unde...
articles.body:
The post How the Crown-of-Thorns Starfish Liquefies Living Coral appeared first on A-Z Animals .

Crown-of-thorns starfish are predatory starfish. They do not feed on sea urchins , barnacles , or even snails like similar species do. Instead, the crown-of-thorns starfish melts living coral for nutrition, often leaving a wave of destruction in its path.

Starfish are carnivores . Many are opportunistic feeders, yet the crown-of-thorns starfish is very specific about what it eats. Their food of choice is coral.

Crown-of-thorns starfish do not simply graze . Instead, they eat coral to the point of the organism's death. To accomplish this, a starfish locates a healthy coral reef to target. Once attached to the reef, the starfish begins to feed.

To feed, the crown-of-thorns starfish pushes its cardiac stomach—the upper part of the stomach where the esophagus connects—out through its mouth, which is located on its underside.

According to the Australian Institute of Marine Science, the stomach spreads out to completely cover the coral polyps . As it does so, it releases enzymes that break down the polyps into a liquid. Once this process is complete, the crown-of-thorns starfish draws the fluid into its body as it retracts its stomach. The only thing left behind is the coral's white skeleton.

Crown-of-Thorns Starfish Can Decimate Coral Reefs

Coral reefs in tropical locales are no stranger to crown-of-thorns starfish. In fact, when populations are under control, crown-of-thorns starfish help prevent fast-growing corals from outcompeting slower-growing corals. This balance helps create a strong and resilient coral reef.

According to a 2022 study , the problem arises when too many crown-of-thorns starfish populate a region. In favorable conditions, there can be up to 1,000 individuals per two acres of marine habitat. Since each adult starfish can consume over 100 square feet of coral per year, large populations can quickly devastate coral reefs.

Because of how quickly the starfish can decimate a coral reef, specific vulnerable reefs are now monitored. This helps ensure that action is taken at the first sign of a crown-of-thorns starfish outbreak, allowing for the removal of the starfish and rehabilitation of the reef before it is permanently destroyed.

Is Human Activity Responsible for Crown-of-Thorns Overpopulation?

Crown-of-thorns starfish are not an invasive species . They are native to the Indo-Pacific. However, their populations can easily grow out of control, and human activity is often to blame.

There are many predators that target crown-of-thorns starfish . However, these same fish are often a favorite among anglers. Consequently, as triggerfish , large wrasse , and even giant snails are depleted from their habitats, crown-of-thorns starfish thrive. The larger their population grows, the more destruction they cause to coral reefs.

Pollution is another cause of starfish population booms . Fertilizer or sewage runoff into the ocean can cause large algal blooms . These blooms provide nutrition to crown-of-thorns larvae, allowing more to survive compared to regions without blooms.

Perhaps one of the ongoing human-caused issues is climate change . While most marine creatures struggle as ocean temperatures increase , crown-of-thorns starfish—and especially their larvae—thrive in these conditions. When temperatures get too warm and coral bleaching occurs, this is an added benefit for the starfish. Dead and dying coral provide an ideal habitat for the starfish to live and create nurseries for their young.

Crown-of-thorns starfish are beneficial to their habitat when their populations can be kept under control. But as the oceans continue to change for the worse, the starfish face fewer obstacles. When their populations become too large, they ruin coral reefs, which are essential for marine biodiversity , coastline protection, and the economic well-being of coastal communities.

articles.title: Over 200 million migratory birds are hitting the sky this week
articles.summary: The central U.S. should be a particular hot spot for birds heading south.
articles.body:
Signs of the waning summer are everywhere. The sun is setting earlier, yellow school buses are emerging from hibernation, and birds are showing up on weather radar once again. The fall migration is in full swing and we humans can follow along with BirdCast.

Over the next two nights (August 25 and 26), BirdCast predicts that over 200 million birds will begin their long journey towards their head for their wintering grounds. Over 300North American bird species are long-distance migrants , meaning they will travel hundreds to thousands of miles annually. These migrations can take days to weeks, depending on the species

BirdCast's daily forecast maps show their predicted nighttime migration patterns that begin roughly three hours after sunset. The brighter and warmer colors represent more birds expected overhead. They are also updated every six hours.

On August 25, expect the largest concentration of birds around Minnesota, North Dakota, and South Dakota.

On Wednesday, August 26, Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas should see the highest concentration of birds.

If you are curious which bird species may be traveling through your area, the dashboard is integrated with Cornell's eBird database . This database uses common bird sightings from the same time in previous years to make predictions.

To make these maps , BirdCast uses weather data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), since their radar picks up large groups. It also uses weather forecasts to predict these nightly migration hotspots. A live map will also go up every night, so users can zero in on what might be going on in the skies where they live. BirdCast is made possible by participating scientists from Cornell University, the University of Massachusetts Amherst, Purdue University, and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, and other contributors.

Typically, birds migrate for two reasons: nests and food. In the Northern Hemisphere, this means heading north during warmer months, when there are more insects and budding plant life to eat. During the spring, many species are also rushing to mate and nest.

Ahead of the colder months, some will return south to avoid freezing temperatures. Earlier in August, a famous, toeless piping plover ( Charadrius melodus ) named Phoenix was spotted back in Florida, after spending the summer over 1,000 miles away in Maine.

However, not all birds head south. Many birds, including mallard ducks ( Anas platyrhynchos ), black-capped chickadees ( Poecile atricapillus ), and the turkey vulture ( Cathartes aura ) don't migrate and fare just fine in snowy conditions.

At least 4,000 bird species (or roughly 40 percent of world's known birds) are regular migrants. The Arctic tern wins the award for longest migration of any bird in the world . These can fly almost 50,000 miles in one year, when traveling between their wintering ground in the Antarctic north to their breeding grounds in the Arctic.

As the migration continues over the next several weeks, there are some easy ways to help make sure that the birds safely make it to their destinations.

Add a film or decals to windows. This can help keep birds from colliding with the glass.

Plant native plants and avoid pesticides when possible. This gives them safe places to land and eat.

Keep cats indoors. This is good advice in general, as housecats can be destructive to the ecosystem , but rings particularly true during bird migration.

Turn off all excess outdoor lights . Too many lights can impact their navigation

articles.title: The bubbling surface of doomed supergiant star Betelgeuse has been revealed like never before
articles.summary: Betelgeuse may be a well-known and often-studied stellar object, but that doesn't mean astronomers aren't capable of capturing this doomed star in a complete...
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

Betelgeuse may be a well-known and often-studied stellar object, but that doesn't mean astronomers aren't capable of capturing this doomed star in a completely new light.

A team of scientists examined the doomed red supergiant star with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), gaining new, highly detailed insights into its turbulent surface. Betelgeuse, located around 600 light-years away, captured the public's attention a few years ago when the rapid and dramatic dimming of the infamous highly evolved star led some scientists to hypothesize that it was about to explode in a spectacular supernova . That hasn't happened, and scientists are now less convinced that this explosion is immediately imminent, but Betelgeuse remains the subject of intense scientific scrutiny.

"Its eventual fate as a supernova makes it fascinating to know what it actually looks like now," team leader Bill Dent, an astronomer at the European Southern Observatory (ESO), said in a statement.

The newly released ALMA images of Betelgeuse, captured in 2023, show bright hotspots on the star's surface and an almost corrugated texture arising from vast amounts of plasma shifting through the star, which has around 20 times the mass of our sun , but is puffed out to around 800 times the size of our star.

The observations show the red supergiant has an atmosphere with a temperature of around 3,680 degrees Fahrenheit (2,030 degrees Celsius), but possesses at least two regions even hotter than this. One of these areas is 980 degrees Fahrenheit (530 degrees Celsius) hotter than the plasma surrounding it.

The uneven nature seen by ALMA is likely the result of massive convective movements in the star, hot plasma rising through the star and generating shockwaves that erupt in the star's atmosphere, creating bright and hot regions. The familiarity of Betelgeuse to astronomers doesn't mean the star isn't capable of delivering surprises too. When the team compared images collected in 2023 to observations from 2015, they were surprised to see a hotspot in the northeast of the stellar disk has persisted for at least seven years, that is much longer than predicted by current stellar models.

The orientation of the hotspots of Betelgeuse also added support to the idea that the red supergiant star is orbited by an elusive companion star .

Astronomers will continue to monitor the hotspots of Betelgeuse with ALMA to determine how fixed they are and how their evolution relates to things like mass loss, and the structure of the star's atmosphere.

That investigation will likely continue until Betelgeuse finally ends its life in a supernova explosion. The team's research has been accepted for publication in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics and is available on the paper repository site arXiv.

articles.title: Elon Musk's space company to build new rocket launching site in Louisiana
articles.summary: Elon Musk's space company plans to spend $100 billion to build a massive new spaceport in Louisiana to launch rockets, state officials and the company announ...
articles.body:
ABBEVILLE, La. (AP) — Elon Musk's space company plans to spend $100 billion to build a massive new spaceport in Louisiana to launch rockets, state officials and the company announced Tuesday.

Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said the deal was a big win for the state and country, likening the impact of the new launch site to the 1803 Louisiana Purchase.

"Today is nothing short of a transformational moment," he told lawmakers and others at a special event to celebrate the deal.

Musk was not there, but he appeared with Landry in a promotional video that played before the Republican governor's speech. SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell also spoke at the event.

The spaceport would be located on 125,000 acres (50,600 hectares) of land formerly owned by Exxon along Louisiana's southern coast about 200 miles (322 km) west of New Orleans in Vermilion Parish. The location provides key advantages, state officials said, including access to abundant natural gas and the ability to launch to a wide range of trajectories.

It would be the company's fourth and largest launch site, playing a key role in ramping up missions of its reusable Starship launch system, according to a news release from Louisiana Economic Development. SpaceX wants to dramatically increase rocket launches as it aims to put more satellites in orbit. The Louisiana site could support thousands of launches each year, the news release said.

State lawmakers had approved sizable tax incentives for the project.

Anne Rolfes, director of the environmental advocacy group, the Louisiana Bucket Brigade, said she was worried the state was moving too fast with a project that would "irrevocably alter" the state's fragile coastline. Construction is expected to begin in 2027, with the first launch targeted for as early as 2029, according to state officials.

"It should be thoughtfully done – with public hearings, and a public process that is transparent and gives people time to understand and consider the project," Rolfes said in a statement. "The speed of the project and the fanfare and bombast make it all highly questionable."

Shotwell said SpaceX planned to keep much of the site undeveloped and would help with restoration and protection efforts, including working to reverse land loss from erosion and "careless use."

"We are committed to doing our part to ensure that this land doesn't disappear," she said.

The company plans to host town halls and other community engagement events in the coming months. State officials said the project would generate 3,000 jobs over a decade.

In June, Musk sold SpaceX shares to the public for the first time in the biggest initial public offering ever. Shares jumped as high as $225 a share, briefly making Musk a trillionaire.

Thanawala reported from Atlanta. Associated Press writer Jack Brook in New Orleans contributed to this report.

articles.title: Brain cells and chemical signals could hold the missing piece of memory
articles.summary: Brain cells and chemical signals could hold the missing piece of memory that today's silicon computers cannot reproduce
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

Brain chemistry may contribute to memory beyond ordinary electrical signalling

AI systems process information without the living cellular environment found inside brains

Astrocytes could play an important role in processing cognitive information

A new scientific model argues that binary code, the 0s and 1s underlying every computer, cannot fully explain how memory works.

Researchers Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Chaim Gilon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem base their model on molecular and cellular evidence.

Their theory, called the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory, proposes that three biological components, not binary switches, are what generate genuine memory.

A chemical basis for how memory actually forms

Unlike a silicon chip storing information as binary states, the tripartite model proposes that memory arises through three separate biological elements interacting.

These elements include brain cells, particularly astrocytes, interacting with neurons, along with the molecular environment surrounding those individual cells directly.

A third component involves specific chemicals, such as metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters, circulating continuously throughout the brain's living tissue.

The researchers suggest that living brains may do more than simply transmit electrical signals between individual neurons scattered across tissue.

They may also write and read certain kinds of information chemically, a process with no clear equivalent inside a silicon processor.

Astrocytes, abundant brain cells that interact closely with neurons, occupy a particularly important place within this newly proposed scientific model.

Marx and Gilon propose that clusters of astrocytes participate in processing cognitive information alongside neurons and the surrounding cellular environment.

A central part of their argument holds that biological memories are never simply pieces of stored logical information by themselves.

They argue that biological memory carries an emotional dimension that no binary code stored inside a computer's memory bank can replicate.

Their model treats chemical messengers, including neurotransmitters, as essential parts of the mechanism by which cognitive information becomes fully encoded.

What the chemistry of memory means for AI

Both computers and biological brains can store and retrieve information, though their underlying mechanisms may differ in fundamental ways.

In a computer, information ultimately carries a physical aspect that is encoded directly into its silicon hardware and internal circuitry.

Marx and Gilon ask whether biological memory also carries a physical aspect, though one rooted in living cells and organic chemistry.

That distinction grows increasingly relevant as AI systems become more capable of performing tasks tied closely to human logical reasoning.

Their paper directly challenges the assumption that greater computational power and complexity alone would necessarily produce biological-like consciousness in machines.

The researchers argue that purely electronic systems lack the biological infrastructure and emotional processes characteristic of living, breathing organisms entirely.

Their argument is not that AI cannot perform increasingly sophisticated intellectual tasks as computing power keeps expanding rapidly each year.

Rather, it raises a more fundamental question about whether intelligent behaviour equals the biological processes producing memory, emotion, and thought.

articles.title: Rare Bird of Prey Nests Again in Secret U.K. Location After Years with No Successful Breeding
articles.summary: The Montagu’s Harrier had shown no evidence of successful breeding in the U.K. between 2020 and 2024
articles.body:
A male Montagu's Harrier raised six chicks across two nests, marking a rare conservation success in the U.K.

Conservationists fitted two chicks with satellite tags to study their migration and improve protection efforts

The species faces threats from climate change and farming practices as their nests are hidden on the ground

The United Kingdom's rarest bird of prey has pulled off a rare conservation win!

According to the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), a male Montagu's Harrier, also known as "AU" by conservationists, bred with two females this year and reared six chicks across two nests on an English farmland. Per the BBC , this marks the second year that the species has successfully nested in the same undisclosed location, where four chicks hatched last year.

The milestone matters because the birds have come perilously close to vanishing from the U.K. Montagu's Harriers were added to the Red List of the country's most at-risk birds in 2021, and successful nests dropped from a high of nine in 2011 to no evidence of successful breeding at all between 2020 and 2024.

"We are doing our absolute utmost to save this iconic species in the U.K. and are delighted with six flying juveniles this year," an RSPB spokesperson told the BBC.

Officials say keeping the chicks alive took a group effort. The organization highlighted careful monitoring, carried out with the farmers whose land the birds nested on, which allowed the nests to be fenced off from ground predators like foxes.

The lone male, meanwhile, worked overtime to feed both nests of hungry chicks. Granted exclusive access to the nest, the BBC witnessed some of the raptors' striking feeding behavior, in which the male drops prey in midair and the female rolls upside down to snatch it in her talons.

Experts note that the slender, long-winged birds make an annual migration to Africa for the winter before returning to Europe to nest over the summer, often in agricultural fields. However, little is known about what juveniles do once they leave the nest, which is why, for the first time, the RSPB fitted two of this year's chicks with satellite tags.

"It will allow us for the first time ever to work out where they're going, what migration route, how long they'll spend there, and will they come back to the U.K. in the first year or the second year," said Mark Thomas, head of investigations at the RSPB. "All of that information is the bit that's missing from the jigsaw."

The tags may also help protect the birds, whose nests sit on the ground, hidden among crops, and are vulnerable to farm machinery.

"This is a species right on the brink, and climate change is not helping that," Thomas added, noting the local harvest came about a month earlier this year than in the past. "It almost puts any Montagu's harrier nest at the peril of inadvertently being destroyed by farm machinery."

Conservationists have asked birders to watch for the young harriers and report any sightings to the RSPB.

articles.title: Deep Sea Scientists Hunting a Shipwreck Accidentally Stumbled Across The Ocean's Own Backrooms
articles.summary: Is there no corner of this Earth our junk does not reach?
articles.body:
More than 5,000 feet beneath the surface of the Gulf of Mexico, scientists encountered a truly alien landscape that might just haunt your dreams.

It was 2017, and a team of scientists from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) were on the hunt for what they thought would be a shipwreck , perhaps containing a lost archaeological trove .

The remotely operated dive was part of an expedition aboard the Okeanos Explorer to map and survey the Gulf, led by marine biologist Diva Amon and echinodermologist Charles Messing.

The boat's sonar had picked up on some kind of structure about 1.5 kilometers (0.9 miles) down. It had the hallmarks of a sunken ship: a large structure surrounded by some loose, smaller ones.

"Today is truly a day of exploration as we send the ROV (remotely-operated vehicle) over to this unknown sonar target," one crew member said as the team guided their ROV towards the wreck.

From the shadows of the Gulf's seafloor, an eerie landscape emerged.

A barren, sandy plain littered with rusted, white cubes – some busted open with the impact of falling, their plastic intestines and copper arteries exposed.

The oddly unsettling imagery feels a little like the ROV has passed through into the deep sea's ' backrooms '.

Zooming in on the scene, a metal tablet of text emerged, encrusted with sand and oxidized metal ooze.

Parts of this misplaced script can just be made out: "To Operate"; "For Personal Safety"; "Problem Solving…".

The dot points that follow each heading, however, were mostly illegible.

Then, looming out of the deep blue, the crew encountered the mother of all cuboids: a crumpled red shipping container, with a clutch of yet more white cubes spilling from its flayed side.

The cubes were a lost payload of white goods: fridges, freezers, washing machines. The inscribed tablet, a set of instructions for doing the laundry.

"I don't think the spin cycle is going to be working on it," one crew member commented , to an eruption of laughter.

A sticker on one of the appliances suggests it originated at General Electric's Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky.

"Other appliances were scattered nearby as well as further afield, forming what we had assumed was a 'debris field'," the official dive notes state .

"The container ID number was ITLU733016 [0], with a series of other identifying markings. The cargo appeared to include a variety of brands (RCA, GE, etc.) and was without packaging, suggesting that the cargo was going to be recycled."

But the container never made it across the waves.

"This is a bit surreal," a crew member mused as the ROV panned across the mod con graveyard.

"We are at 1.5 kilometers… in the deep sea. And here we are, moving through a field of just freezers, fridges and washing machines.

"You think of the deep sea as a fairly untouched place, but this is just a reminder that it really is not. We still do manage to have an impact on this very alien area and ecosystem."

The NOAA team speculated the container could have come off a ship in stormy weather.

According to World Shipping Council data , a few hundred to over 1,000 containers are lost at sea each year, out of approximately 280 million transported.

In a recent report of the 2025 figures, they note that severe weather increases the likelihood that freight boats will drop some cargo as they encounter rougher seas.

Even without storms, warmer-than-usual ocean temperatures can increase wave energy.

"Most people out there probably don't realize how much stuff ends up in the ocean," a NOAA crew member said .

"The research has suggested that lost containers could take hundreds of years to fully degrade in the deep ocean if not more," another crew member added .

In the meantime, some animals have decided to call these bizarre benthic backrooms their home.

Corals and hydroids cling to the metal structures, their soft bodies rippling in response to the passing ROV.

A large fish even sheltered in the container's shadows.

The NOAA crew nicknamed the wreck 'Deep Clean'.

These kinds of ROV missions are part of NOAA's continuing work to explore the deep ocean.

ROV missions are operated by a crew of scientists and technicians aboard a ship on the water's surface, who remotely guide a submersible robot to the depths.

The ROV is connected to the ship by a long cable, through which commands are sent, and data (like the live video feed) is returned.

This is why we can hear the scientists reacting in real-time: their voices are recorded along with the live feed.

Related: 'Most Isolated Environments': Microplastics Are Finding Their Way Down to Deep-Sea Hydrothermal Vents

This allows them to take important audio notes on what they are seeing in real-time (although this particular clip was compiled from the raw, live footage, after the expedition).

The live nature of these ROV feeds also offers us a window into the crew's reactions to some of the weird and wonderful things they find while exploring these uncharted waters.

articles.title: FDA authorizes Abbott's wearable to monitor ketone and glucose in diabetes patients
articles.summary: Food and Drug Administration said on Tuesday it authorized Abbott Laboratories' glucose monitor, ‌making it the first device that continuously monitors both...
articles.body:
Aug 25 (Reuters) - The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said on Tuesday it authorized Abbott Laboratories' glucose monitor, ‌making it the first device that continuously monitors both ‌ketone levels and blood sugar.

• The device branded as ​Libre Duo 10 Day is designed for a 10-day wear period for people aged 2 years and older living with diabetes.

• The biowearable is designed to alert people of rising ketones that ‌can lead to ⁠a diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) emergency, a serious health complication for people with diabetes.

• Unlike earlier ketone tests ⁠that offered only separate, one-time readings, Abbott's device continuously monitors both ketone and glucose levels, displaying real-time trends.

• The device can ​send automatic ​alerts, which may help patients ​and caregivers recognize rising ketones ‌before DKA becomes a medical emergency.

• "If glucose is the speedometer, ketones are like the check engine light—providing an alert that something may need attention," said Chris Scoggins, executive vice president of Abbott's diabetes care business.

• The device brings both glucose ‌and ketone levels together in a ​single dashboard, providing a more complete ​picture to help people ​with diabetes make more informed decisions, added Scoggins.

• ‌Abbott is working with leading pump ​companies to ​enable automated insulin delivery systems to connect with the sensors.

• The company said the device integrates with the Libre ​app and expects ‌Libre Duo 10 Day to work with devices from ​Insulet and Tandem in 2027.

(Reporting by Christy Santhosh in ​Bengaluru; Editing by Vijay Kishore)

articles.body: For generations, a two-acre plot of land along the MississippiâTennessee state line served as both sanctuary and survival for Krystal Polkâs family. They raised chickens and pigs, harvested onions and herbs, and traded homegrown peaches for pears. But after what is reported to be decades of weathering racial hostility and hardship to keep the property in the family, an unrelenting industrial hum has finally forced them out, according to a report by CBS News. "We lived a very simplistic life," Polk, 52, told CBS News.The history of the Southaven homestead was anything but simple. Polk explained that her ancestors acquired the land "before people of color were allowed to have land." When her parents first moved onto the property decades ago, they found the letters "KKK" scrawled at the bottom of the hill. Through generations of systemic barriers and intimidation, the family held firm.Their way of life unraveled about a year ago with the sudden arrival of a noisy new neighbor directly across the street: a massive power plant installed to run Elon Muskâs nearby artificial intelligence data centers in the Memphis area. The facilityâs constant noise drove the family away from their longtime home. Today, the property sits largely abandoned, overshadowed by the persistent mechanical drone.The site is part of a broader infrastructure buildout powering Elon Musk's data operations, which has ignited fierce pushback from Southaven residents who argue the high-output generators have brought unmanageable noise and air pollution into their residential community.Here's the petition by the resident-run Safe and Sound Coalition calling to shut down the power plantWeâre a Mississippi grassroots coalition-turned non-profit raising concerns about xAI. xAI's Southaven power plant, which borders both Horn Lake and Memphis and is intended to provide energy for their data center(s), is surrounded by our homes, churches, parks, and schools.This project has raised serious concerns about transparency and regulatory accountability, and whether the public is truly being heard in decisions that directly affect our health, environment, and quality of life.We have worked to increase transparencyâ providing accessible information and ensuring our neighbors are not left in the dark as this project continues to move forward at an alarming pace. We are advocating for our communities' rights to clean air, quiet nights, responsible growth, and honest leadership.If youâre frustrated, concerned, or just want to understand whatâs really going onâ youâre not alone. We believe our communities deserve better. Join us to take action, stay informed, and protect our communities.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Ancient shark graveyard discovered in Egypt reveals 5 extinct species from dinosaur era
articles.summary: Scientists have made a rare discovery in Egypt's desert, uncovering a shark graveyard of now-extinct species left frozen in time, waiting to be found.
articles.body:
Five extinct shark species from the Cretaceous period were found in Egypt.

The Cretaceous period had sea levels ranging from 320 to 850 feet higher than today.

EGYPT – Scientists have made a rare discovery in Egypt's desert, uncovering a shark graveyard of now-extinct species left frozen in time, waiting to be found.

Archaeologists in Egypt's southwestern desert dug phosphate beds from the Duwi Formation, a Late Cretaceous deposit, and found a former tropical marine environment that preserved these fossils.

This geological dig site preserves marine vertebrates and fossils, allowing experts to connect certain physical attributes correctly.

Ancient 'Lost World' Could Rewrite History For How First Americans Arrived 13,000 Years Ago

The result is a new assemblage of extinct lamniform sharks, some of which represent the first fossil record for Egypt and Africa , according to Cretaceous Research.

Within these phosphate beds, archaeologists uncovered five extinct shark species named Cretalamna cf. C . maroccana, Scapanorhynchus cf. S . raphiodon, Serratolamna cf. S. serrata, Squalicorax bassanii, and Squalicorax pristodontus .

Officials also found 14 fossilized teeth belonging to the sharks.

This was the Late Cretaceous period, when sea levels were much higher than today, ranging from around 320 to 850 feet higher than now.

Evidence suggests life probably began in the ocean at least 3.5 billion years ago, with the first organisms being single-celled microbes, and for 2.3 billion years, life consisted of only this.

Watch: Sandbar Shark Swims Off Rhode Island Coast As Numbers Across New England Surge

Until around 1.2 billion years ago, when more complex multicellular organisms evolved, and since then, more life forms have appeared and evolved, but not continuously, as some don't survive the changes of this world .

See It: Ancient Tomb And Artifacts Uncovered During Expansion Of Italian Pasta Factory

Through further study and more discoveries in this region, officials hope to shed new light on the paleodiversity and secrets these fossils hide about various periods in time and the environment they inhabited.

articles.title: Alfalfa Sprouts Were Linked to E. Coli and Salmonella at the Same Time — Here’s How That’s Possible
articles.summary: Among the 55 cases reported in the outbreaks, at least two people were infected with both bacteria.
articles.body:
Everything Sprouts recalled select lots of Everything Sprouts and Calco alfalfa sprouts because of potential E. coli and Salmonella contamination. The outbreak has been linked to 55 illnesses across 15 states and four hospitalizations.

Alfalfa sprouts are considered a higher-risk food because the warm, moist conditions used to germinate the seeds also favor bacterial growth. Bacteria on contaminated seeds can grow during germination and become trapped within microscopic tissues, making them difficult to wash away.

Consumers should dispose of recalled sprouts and clean and sanitize any surfaces or containers they touched. Older adults, young children, pregnant individuals, and immunocompromised people should avoid raw or lightly cooked sprouts.

The summer of foodborne outbreaks now includes an alfalfa sprout recall linked to two foodborne illnesses. Everything Sprouts, LLC has recalled select lots of its alfalfa sprouts sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands due to potential contamination with E. coli and Salmonella .

To date, 55 cases linked to the recall have been reported across 15 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Four people have been hospitalized in connection with the outbreak, and at least two have been infected with both E. coli and Salmonella .

"Everything Sprouts became aware of reports of illnesses from federal and state agencies," the company said in a statement . "During this outbreak, we have tested our products daily and have not received any positive lab results. We continue to work closely with public health officials to investigate the source of this potential issue and will provide updates as they become available."

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) maintains the full list of recalled products, including lot numbers and bar codes.

The recall is raising many questions about how you can get two illnesses from one food. As you can imagine, "it has been very rare to have more than one bacterial pathogen causing outbreaks and recalls in the past," says Francisco Diez-Gonzalez , PhD, director of the Center for Food Safety at the University of Georgia. But alfalfa sprouts have unique characteristics that make them ideal breeding grounds for bacteria — even two types at once, according to Kalmia E. Kniel , PhD, professor and chair of microbial food safety at the University of Delaware.

How can alfalfa sprouts be contaminated with two types of bacterial pathogens at once?

"Sprouts are often considered higher-risk products," Kniel says. The seeds are germinated to create sprouts in moist, humid, warm environments, and these are the same conditions that favor the growth of bacteria, including Salmonella and E. coli , she explains. It's usually thought that the fields where the alfalfa seeds were grown could have been contaminated by irrigation or runoff water, soil, or animal waste, Diez-Gonzalez says.

"There is often concern that the seeds are contaminated," Kniel says. As a result, the seeds are often soaked in chlorinated water . "But soaking the seeds in chlorinated water will not completely inactivate the pathogens, as the bacteria are protected in the crevices of the seeds," Kniel says.

Related: Recalls Are Rising: This Is How Food Safety Experts Decide What's Safe to Eat

Multiple alfalfa sprout recalls have been linked to E. coli or Salmonella separately, Diez-Gonzalez says. "According to most of the evidence, the bacteria can be present in the seeds after contamination of the fields where the alfalfa plants are grown as a source of seeds," he says. But when the seeds are germinated, the bacteria can grow into the sprouts.

At that point, "bacteria present on the seed shell can become trapped within microscopic tissues, making them impossible to wash away," Kniel says. "These aren't two separate contamination events," says Amesh A. Adalja , MD, an infectious disease expert and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. "The seed is the shared vehicle."

What are the symptoms of an E. coli and Salmonella co-infection?

It depends. "These bacteria attach to different receptors, provoke different inflammatory responses," Adalja says.

These illnesses can look "indistinguishable without testing," according to Adalja. However, he says that someone with an E. coli and Salmonella co-infection would likely experience cramps, diarrhea, fever, and sometimes bloody stool, given the "overlap" in symptoms between E. coli and Salmonella infections.

Related: The Food Recall System Is Broken, and Experts Say We're All at Risk

Doctors would typically only know if you have two infections if you're given a multiplex PCR gastrointestinal panel that tests your stool sample against several potential pathogens, Adalja explains.

While these co-infections aren't common, Adalja says they may have occurred in the past more often than people realize. "Co-infections almost certainly occurred in earlier sprout outbreaks, but clinicians weren't using tools in a way that would find them," he says.

When did the E. coli and Salmonella outbreaks start?

Illnesses linked to the outbreak began on May 31 and have continued since then, according to the CDC .

According to the CDC, 76% of the 34 interviewed patients said they'd eaten alfalfa sprouts before getting sick. Epidemiological evidence and traceback information from restaurants and grocery stores suggest that Everything Sprouts could be fueling the outbreak.

What should you do if you have recalled alfalfa sprouts?

If you have the recalled products at home, the FDA and CDC recommend disposing of them. Then, clean and sanitize any surfaces or containers the sprouts may have touched.

Alfalfa sprouts remain a high-risk food regardless of whether there is a recall, Kniel points out. "Vulnerable populations — older adults, young children, pregnant individuals, and anyone immunocompromised — should avoid raw or lightly cooked sprouts," she says.

If you really love alfalfa sprouts but want to lower your risk of getting sick under ordinary circumstances, Diez-Gonzalez suggests cooking your sprouts before eating them.

Fast Facts: Alfalfa sprouts linked to E. coli and Salmonella outbreaks

Which alfalfa sprout products are being recalled? These products have been recalled as part of the outbreak, according to the FDA :

Everything Sprouts and Calco-branded alfalfa sprouts (5 ounces) with lot numbers 222, 223, 225, 226, or 230 and bar codes 860014523113, 860014523120, or 850079470149

Everything Sprouts Crunchy Protein Sprout Mix (5-ounce cups) with lot numbers 222, 223, 226, and 230

Everything Sprouts Zesty Garlic Mix (5-ounce cups) with lot numbers 222, 223, 225, 226, and 230

Where have illnesses linked to the recalled sprouts been reported? Infections have been detected in these states, according to the CDC : Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Washington, and Wisconsin

"There is often concern that the seeds are contaminated," Kniel says. As a result, the seeds are often soaked in chlorinated water . "But soaking the seeds in chlorinated water will not completely inactivate the pathogens, as the bacteria are protected in the crevices of the seeds," Kniel says.
Related: Recalls Are Rising: This Is How Food Safety Experts Decide What's Safe to Eat

Multiple alfalfa sprout recalls have been linked to E. coli or Salmonella separately, Diez-Gonzalez says. "According to most of the evidence, the bacteria can be present in the seeds after contamination of the fields where the alfalfa plants are grown as a source of seeds," he says. But when the seeds are germinated, the bacteria can grow into the sprouts.

At that point, "bacteria present on the seed shell can become trapped within microscopic tissues, making them impossible to wash away," Kniel says. "These aren't two separate contamination events," says Amesh A. Adalja , MD, an infectious disease expert and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. "The seed is the shared vehicle."
What are the symptoms of an E. coli and Salmonella co-infection?
It depends. "These bacteria attach to different receptors, provoke different inflammatory responses," Adalja says.

These illnesses can look "indistinguishable without testing," according to Adalja. However, he says that someone with an E. coli and Salmonella co-infection would likely experience cramps, diarrhea, fever, and sometimes bloody stool, given the "overlap" in symptoms between E. coli and Salmonella infections.
Related: The Food Recall System Is Broken, and Experts Say We're All at Risk
Doctors would typically only know if you have two infections if you're given a multiplex PCR gastrointestinal panel that tests your stool sample against several potential pathogens, Adalja explains.

While these co-infections aren't common, Adalja says they may have occurred in the past more often than people realize. "Co-infections almost certainly occurred in earlier sprout outbreaks, but clinicians weren't using tools in a way that would find them," he says.
When did the E. coli and Salmonella outbreaks start?
Illnesses linked to the outbreak began on May 31 and have continued since then, according to the CDC .

According to the CDC, 76% of the 34 interviewed patients said they'd eaten alfalfa sprouts before getting sick. Epidemiological evidence and traceback information from restaurants and grocery stores suggest that Everything Sprouts could be fueling the outbreak.
What should you do if you have recalled alfalfa sprouts?
If you have the recalled products at home, the FDA and CDC recommend disposing of them. Then, clean and sanitize any surfaces or containers the sprouts may have touched.

Alfalfa sprouts remain a high-risk food regardless of whether there is a recall, Kniel points out. "Vulnerable populations — older adults, young children, pregnant individuals, and anyone immunocompromised — should avoid raw or lightly cooked sprouts," she says.
If you really love alfalfa sprouts but want to lower your risk of getting sick under ordinary circumstances, Diez-Gonzalez suggests cooking your sprouts before eating them.
Fast Facts: Alfalfa sprouts linked to E. coli and Salmonella outbreaks
Which alfalfa sprout products are being recalled? These products have been recalled as part of the outbreak, according to the FDA :
Everything Sprouts and Calco-branded alfalfa sprouts (5 ounces) with lot numbers 222, 223, 225, 226, or 230 and bar codes 860014523113, 860014523120, or 850079470149
Everything Sprouts Crunchy Protein Sprout Mix (5-ounce cups) with lot numbers 222, 223, 226, and 230
Everything Sprouts Zesty Garlic Mix (5-ounce cups) with lot numbers 222, 223, 225, 226, and 230

Where have illnesses linked to the recalled sprouts been reported? Infections have been detected in these states, according to the CDC : Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Washington, and Wisconsin

articles.title: New Map Shows Which U.S. States Will Have 'Good' View of Thursday's Lunar Eclipse
articles.summary: A new map has emerged for the near-total lunar eclipse.
articles.body:
Just part of the United States will have a good view of the near-total lunar eclipse this Thursday, August 27.

Roughly half of the United States will have "good" to "okay" views of the lunar event this Thursday, while the other half of the country will have "poor" viewing conditions. The near-total lunar eclipse is set to begin on Thursday night.

According to astronomy.com , the eclipse will begin at 9:23 p.m. E.T., as the Moon first enters the outer part of Earth's shadow, the penumbra. However, the best viewing conditions will come at 10:33 p.m. E.T. That's when the Moon will first pass into the umbra, which is the darker, inner portion of our planet's shadow — and the partial eclipse begins before midnight.

Ultimately, not everyone in the United States will have a good view of it. But many will!

U.S. states with "good" viewing conditions of the near-total lunar eclipse are as follows:

U.S. states with "okay" viewing conditions include:

And, finally, the U.S. states with "bad" viewing conditions include:

Unlike solar eclipses, you can watch the lunar eclipse with your naked eye. You don't need any optical aid, as it'll be viewable with just your eyes alone.

Lunar eclipses also progress slowly, so there's not a huge rush to look at the sky on Thursday evening. The lunar eclipse process will be viewable for much of Thursday evening heading into Friday morning, August 28.

However, this is the last lunar eclipse until February of 2027. And the next one after that isn't until August of 2027.

So, if you can get to a viewpoint of the lunar eclipse, it'll be your last opportunity to do so for a while.

articles.title: NASA Can't Rescue The Satellite That Was Going To Rescue Another Satellite After All
articles.summary: The plan was for the Link satellite to fly over to Swift, grab onto it, and haul it back up into a stable orbit. Unfortunately, that's not what happened.
articles.body:
NASA and Katalyst Space Technologies have jointly announced that the latter's Link satellite will no longer attempt to grab and boost the former's Swift satellite back into stable orbit. To put it another way: The attempt to rescue the rescue satellite could not rescue the rescue satellite, which will no longer be able to rescue the other satellite, which now cannot be rescued at all, and neither can the rescue satellite. Despite the apparent failure, both NASA and Katalyst still see positives in the fact that an attempt could even be put together in under a year, something that would have been impossible not all that long ago.

The backstory here is that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a NASA space telescope launched in 2004 to study gamma-ray bursts, decayed out of orbit and began to fall back to Earth. In fairness, the mission was only supposed to last two years, so Swift did pretty well overall. As a test and flex of America's growing commercial space capability, last year NASA gave Katalyst $30 million to see if they could get a rescue attempt together. The plan was for the Link satellite to fly over to Swift, grab onto it, and haul it back up into a stable orbit. Unfortunately, just a few weeks after making it into orbit itself, Link went into a terrible spin . Katalyst made a heroic effort to use its remaining propulsion to arrest the spin and continue the mission, but now, the towel has been thrown. That doesn't mean it's all over, though.

On July 25, Link transited into a known communications black-out zone, which should have only lasted an hour or so. Somewhere in that hour, something went horrifically wrong, and the rescue satellite went into a rapid multi-axis spin. Katalyst never formally announced what went wrong, though the New York Times reports that it was due to faulty maneuvering thrusters. In any case, the loss of communication resulted in a cascade of other failures, including the reaction wheels and thrusters, which control where the spacecraft is pointed. Katalyst tried to make up for these losses by using the remaining reaction wheel, thrusters, and electric propulsion system. That did appear to bring Link out of spin and back into regular communications contact.

Unfortunately, doing so ate up a bunch of the precious xenon fuel onboard. There just isn't enough of that fuel left to safely attempt to boost Swift back into orbit. So, rather than risk a crash, the rescue mission is off. Instead, Link will attempt to get near Swift and perform maneuvers around it. This might seem like dancing on Swift's grave, but the idea is to test out whatever Link can still manage and pass on those learnings to future space operations. Maybe one day, NASA and Katalyst will try again with another satellite, and the lessons of Link will lead them to success. "We knew this was a high-risk, high-reward mission – a first-of-its kind attempt," said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director, Astrophysics Division, NASA Headquarters in Washington . "But we knew the takeaways from this mission would be worthwhile either way."

This is the end for Swift and its multi-decade survey of gamma ray bursts, though. NASA expects it to re-enter Earth's atmosphere sometime this year, where it will mostly burn up. Some pieces will strike the surface, though. The space agency told the NYT that "the risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely." That sounds like just hoping for the best, which is more or less how most satellites crash back to our planet . As we send more and more satellites into orbit every year , we're going to need to have a serious discussion about how we retire them. Or, maybe, how we rescue them.
