articles.title: In 2025, 11-year-old Touren Pope spotted a fossil exposed on the ground in Wyoming; it turned out to be a nearly complete 48-million-year-old turtle shell, and he was allowed to name it
articles.summary: Science News: What began as a routine family rock-hounding trip in southwest Wyoming turned into a paleontological headline when 11-year-old Touren Pope noticed som.
articles.body: What began as a routine family rock-hounding trip in southwest Wyoming turned into a paleontological headline when 11-year-old Touren Pope noticed something unusual poking out of the ground. What heâd spotted was the fossilized shell of a softshell turtle that lived nearly 48 million years ago, preserved in the Bridger Formation of the Greater Green River Basin. After Touren and his grandparents reported the find to the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), experts confirmed its significance and arranged a careful excavation. In recognition of his discovery, Touren was given the rare honor of naming the fossil. Here's the complete story, based on BLM and regional news coverage of the discovery:A keen eye on public landTouren Pope, a sixth-grader from Nevada, was visiting his grandparents in Wyoming in the fall of 2025 when the family set out to search for interesting rocks and minerals on BLM-managed land near Rock Springs. While scanning the ground, he noticed a dark, rounded object that didnât look like an ordinary stone. Following the rules for vertebrate fossils on public land, the family left the specimen in place and contacted the BLM Rock Springs Field Office.BLM paleontology staff quickly recognised the potential importance of the find. J.P. Cavigelli, a paleontologist and museum specialist with the agency, said that within minutes they could tell it was a fairly complete turtle shell worth collecting. Because exposed fossils can deteriorate rapidly once they reach the surface, timing was critical. âIf we donât find them in time, they usually decompose quickly once they reach the surface,â BLM archaeologist Craig Thomas noted.Excavating âLittle TimmyâIn September 2025, a team from the Tate Geological Museum in Casper, working with BLM approval, returned to the site with Touren and his grandparents to fully excavate the fossil.The excavation revealed that only the turtleâs upper shell, or carapace, remained, but it was nearly complete and remarkably well preserved. The shell was carefully transported to the Tate Geological Museum, a BLM-approved repository, where it is being cleaned, stabilized, and prepared for research and possible public display.As a special thank-you, officials allowed Touren to give the fossil an official name. He chose âLittle Timmy,â a moniker that has since appeared in news stories and museum communications about the specimen.By early 2026, Touren even came to the museum to help collections staff clean the fossil, further cementing his connection to the find. A window into a warm, river-filled past During the Eocene Epoch, roughly 48 million years ago, the Greater Green River Basin looked very different than the semi-arid landscape of today. It was much warmer then, with rivers and streams running throughout, supporting a bustling ecosystem of fish, crocodiles, turtles and other animals. Their remains were buried in sediments for millions of years, eventually turning into fossils within rock layers such as the Bridger Formation.Natural erosion later exposed Little Timmyâs shell at the surface, where it waited for someone with a sharp eye to notice. BLM officials say the turtle was likely a softshell species in the trionychid family, whose modern relatives still live in rivers and lakes today. Softshell turtles have flatter, more flexible shells than many other turtles, and their fossils offer clues about ancient aquatic environments and how these animals evolved over time.Why public-land rules matter for fossilsTourenâs discovery also highlights why rules around fossils on public land exist. Vertebrate fossils on BLM-managed areas are considered part of the nationâs scientific and cultural heritage, and removing them without authorization can destroy important context for researchers.By leaving the shell in place and notifying the BLM, Touren and his family ensured that professionals could document the site, collect the specimen properly, and preserve it in a museum where it can be studied and shared with the public.The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land in the United States, much of it in the West, where erosion constantly exposes new fossils. Agency paleontologists rely on visitors to report potential finds so that significant specimens arenât lost to weather, vandalism, or unregulated collecting. In that sense, Tourenâs story is both a personal triumph and a model for how the public can help protect ancient history.From rock hound to fossil namesakeFor an 11-year-old, being credited with uncovering a 48-million-year-old turtle is extraordinary. For scientists, Little Timmy is a valuable data point in reconstructing the Eocene ecosystems of the Green River Basin.And for the museums, the specimen is a future exhibit that can inspire other young rock hounds to carefully examine the ground underfoot. Tourenâs discovery reminds us that significant scientific contributions arenât always made in university labs or with large field crews. Sometimes, they begin with a curious kid, a family outing, and the choice to do the right thing when something ancient and fragile emerges from the dirt.

Because exposed fossils can deteriorate rapidly once they reach the surface, timing was critical. âIf we donât find them in time, they usually decompose quickly once they reach the surface,â BLM archaeologist Craig Thomas noted.Excavating âLittle TimmyâIn September 2025, a team from the Tate Geological Museum in Casper, working with BLM approval, returned to the site with Touren and his grandparents to fully excavate the fossil.The excavation revealed that only the turtleâs upper shell, or carapace, remained, but it was nearly complete and remarkably well preserved. The shell was carefully transported to the Tate Geological Museum, a BLM-approved repository, where it is being cleaned, stabilized, and prepared for research and possible public display.As a special thank-you, officials allowed Touren to give the fossil an official name. He chose âLittle Timmy,â a moniker that has since appeared in news stories and museum communications about the specimen.By early 2026, Touren even came to the museum to help collections staff clean the fossil, further cementing his connection to the find. A window into a warm, river-filled past During the Eocene Epoch, roughly 48 million years ago, the Greater Green River Basin looked very different than the semi-arid landscape of today. It was much warmer then, with rivers and streams running throughout, supporting a bustling ecosystem of fish, crocodiles, turtles and other animals. Their remains were buried in sediments for millions of years, eventually turning into fossils within rock layers such as the Bridger Formation.Natural erosion later exposed Little Timmyâs shell at the surface, where it waited for someone with a sharp eye to notice. BLM officials say the turtle was likely a softshell species in the trionychid family, whose modern relatives still live in rivers and lakes today. Softshell turtles have flatter, more flexible shells than many other turtles, and their fossils offer clues about ancient aquatic environments and how these animals evolved over time.Why public-land rules matter for fossilsTourenâs discovery also highlights why rules around fossils on public land exist. Vertebrate fossils on BLM-managed areas are considered part of the nationâs scientific and cultural heritage, and removing them without authorization can destroy important context for researchers.By leaving the shell in place and notifying the BLM, Touren and his family ensured that professionals could document the site, collect the specimen properly, and preserve it in a museum where it can be studied and shared with the public.The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land in the United States, much of it in the West, where erosion constantly exposes new fossils. Agency paleontologists rely on visitors to report potential finds so that significant specimens arenât lost to weather, vandalism, or unregulated collecting. In that sense, Tourenâs story is both a personal triumph and a model for how the public can help protect ancient history.From rock hound to fossil namesakeFor an 11-year-old, being credited with uncovering a 48-million-year-old turtle is extraordinary. For scientists, Little Timmy is a valuable data point in reconstructing the Eocene ecosystems of the Green River Basin.And for the museums, the specimen is a future exhibit that can inspire other young rock hounds to carefully examine the ground underfoot. Tourenâs discovery reminds us that significant scientific contributions arenât always made in university labs or with large field crews. Sometimes, they begin with a curious kid, a family outing, and the choice to do the right thing when something ancient and fragile emerges from the dirt.

articles.title: 1,500-year-old child burial unearthed in Peru with whistles, a rattle and a striking sculptural vessel, archaeologists uncover clues to an ancient civilisationâs rituals
articles.summary: Science News: Archaeologists working at the Huacas de Moche Archaeological Complex in northern Peru have uncovered the burial of an infant estimated to be about 1,5.
articles.body: Archaeologists working at the Huacas de Moche Archaeological Complex in northern Peru have uncovered the burial of an infant estimated to be about 1,500 years old. The child, approximately 1.5 years old, was buried with a funerary assemblage that included two whistles, a rattle and a sculptural vessel. Researchers say the burial displays a pattern characteristic of the Moche culture. According to Peru's Andina news agency, archaeologists discovered the burial in Architectural Complex 61, located in the southern sector of the Moche urban core. Archaeologist Jermi Mejia said the infant's remains were found in a reclining position, with the head facing south and the legs facing north.A carefully arranged burialMejia said the burial was accompanied by four notable objects: two whistles, a rattle and a sculptural vessel. These items provide information about the cultural and funerary practices of the society that inhabited the site around 1,500 years ago. The objects also give archaeologists an opportunity to examine how funerary items were placed alongside the dead. Their exact significance to the Moche, however, cannot be determined from the discovery alone.The burial's location and arrangement add to the archaeological evidence from the site, allowing researchers to examine how funerary practices were carried out within the Moche urban environment.Found in a residential areaThe location of the burial is just as important as the objects found with it. Architectural Complex 61 is situated in the southern sector of the Moche urban core and contains small platforms and partition walls that separated spaces used for different activities. Archaeologists also recovered domestic vessels associated with the abandonment of the space. According to Andina, these objects provide insights into aspects of diet, daily activities and the use of residential areas.That combination of domestic evidence and a child burial gives researchers an opportunity to look beyond the ceremonial spaces of Huacas de Moche. Instead, the excavation is helping researchers examine aspects of life within the residential parts of the ancient settlement. The excavation work includes graphic, elevation, photographic, film and aerial documentation. Researchers will also continue excavating deeper levels to identify changes made to the architecture over time.Understanding the Moche communityThe Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project is focused on expanding knowledge about the population that inhabited the Moche urban core and understanding their daily lives beyond ceremonial spaces, according to project director Carlos Rengifo. The current field season includes three main areas of work: the ceremonial and funerary area, the urban, domestic and residential sector, and production areas.The Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project was established in 1991 as an academic research initiative led by National University of Trujillo faculty members Santiago Uceda and Ricardo Morales. Its study area encompasses the Huacas del Sol y la Luna and the spaces associated with the surrounding adobe structures. The research is funded by the National University of Trujillo, which has supported the project since its creation. The project also includes conservation, tourism and community outreach activities.More clues beneath the surfaceThe newly uncovered burial is part of a wider excavation effort at the archaeological complex. The current stage of work is expected to continue for approximately one month, after which the area will be protected with clean sand against possible rainfall associated with the El NiÃ±o phenomenon. The excavation is helping researchers build a broader picture of the people who lived at Huacas de Moche. While the site is widely associated with its monumental adobe structures, investigations of residential and domestic spaces can provide different clues about everyday life. The infant's burial adds another piece to that picture. Its location, orientation and accompanying objects provide archaeologists with evidence of funerary practices within the Moche urban core.The whistles, rattle and sculptural vessel cannot by themselves reveal exactly what the Moche intended when they were placed beside the child. But together with the burial's characteristic arrangement, they provide researchers with additional evidence for studying the cultural and funerary practices of the society that inhabited Huacas de Moche around 1,500 years ago.

articles.title: 6,500 years ago, someone drilled a human tooth and wore it as a pendant; archaeologists found it sitting in a Serbian museum collection
articles.summary: Science News: It sat on a museum shelf for nearly twenty years, unseen, mistaken for something far more common. But now a closer look at a tiny, worn tooth is givin.
articles.body: It sat on a museum shelf for nearly twenty years, unseen, mistaken for something far more common. But now a closer look at a tiny, worn tooth is giving a remarkable glimpse into how Neolithic people in the Balkans may have remembered, and perhaps even honored, the dead, states an archaeology report by Phys Org. If we go by the report, more than 6,500 years ago, someone drilled a hole through a human canine, threaded it on a cord and probably wore it as a pendant. The bizarre artifact was unearthed at the Neolithic site of Jablanica, in Serbia, and is now regarded as the only reliably documented human tooth ornament from the Neolithic central Balkans, adds the report.A bead that was not a beadIt is mentioned in the study that the tooth was found in field surveys at Jablanica, a settlement belonging to the VinÄa culture, one of the major societies of prehistoric Europe. Pottery, figurines and finely crafted bone tools were also found at the site, south of Belgrade, since its discovery in the late 19th century. When archeologists found the tooth it was already damaged, measuring only 23 millimeters. Its crown had been split by agricultural activity into two parts. The pieces eventually ended up in the Museum of Mladenovac, where they were identified as parts of a bead and largely forgotten for nearly 20 years. That was until archeologist Nemanja MarkoviÄ and his colleague Ana MariÄiÄ examined the object more closely. âI was curious more than surprised at first,â MarkoviÄ said in the report. But upon seeing the unmistakable shape of a human canine, âit was clear that we were looking at something far more unusual than a typical tooth bead.âClues in the toothSince the tooth had been found on the surface rather than in a secure archeological context, its age and history had to be established by detective work. The experts used a combination of visual inspection, microscopy, and X-ray analysis. Evidence of wear on the chewing surface suggested that the tooth had belonged to a middle-aged adult. The root was also in good condition, suggesting that it had not been forcibly removed from a living person. The tooth was likely taken from the remains of someone who had already died and whose skeleton had become sufficiently exposed or accessible for the tooth to be collected. Dating the ornament itself was more difficult. Its drill marks were compared with those on a shell bracelet from Jablanica that is securely dated to about 4700 B.C. The researchers say that similarities in the manufacturing techniques suggest that the tooth pendant dates to roughly the same period, though they note that certainty is impossible for a surface find.A craft of remarkable skillAccording to the experts, there is a good deal of craftsmanship shown in the object as well. Under the microscope MarkoviÄ saw fastidious workmanship that indicated the pendant was no hasty improvised trinket. The drilling was skillful and the surfaces were smooth, which suggests that the object could have been worn for a long time. This is especially impressive as the ornaments seem to have been rare at Jablanica. There have been only two other examples found there, a part of a shell bracelet and another shell pendant. Elsewhere in Europe, human tooth ornaments are also rare. Such examples have occasionally been reported, but none has been firmly established for the Neolithic central Balkans.Memory in a surprising formThe finding poses interesting questions about the relationship between the living and the dead in VinÄa society. It was not merely a biological remnant. Someone had selected it, modified it with careful artistry, and apparently worn it for personal adornment. What it meant, remembrance, identity, status, ancestry or something more intimate, is unknown. The discovery is also a reminder that archeology can sometimes be about asking new questions of old things. The tiny tooth from Jablanica tells a much bigger story: that in Neolithic Europe, human remains may not have been confined to graves. It seems that at least here part of a dead person was turned into an object that could be kept close to the body, a striking expression of memory, meaning and the continuing connection between the living and the dead.

articles.title: Columbia engineers built a pigment-free polymer coating filled with microscopic air pores; under Arizona desert sun, the coated surface stayed about 6Â°C below ambient air
articles.summary: Science News: As temperatures rise during hot weather, keeping buildings and other structures cool can require large amounts of energy. Air conditioners are a commo.
articles.body: As temperatures rise during hot weather, keeping buildings and other structures cool can require large amounts of energy. Air conditioners are a common way to deal with the heat, but they consume electricity and need access to cooling systems and, in some cases, coolants that can affect the environment.Researchers at Columbia Engineering have created a polymer coating that can be applied like paint and uses microscopic air voids instead of white pigments. According to the University's engineering department, the coating can reflect sunlight while also releasing heat towards the sky, allowing the surface to cool below the surrounding air temperature.The researchers tested the coating in different environments. Under the warm, dry conditions of the Arizona desert, the coated surface became about 6Â°C cooler than the ambient air. On the ther hand, in a foggy, tropical environment in Bangladesh, it achieved cooling of about 3Â°C below the surrounding air.The work is based on a process called passive daytime radiative cooling (PDRC). It allows a surface to cool without using an external energy source by reflecting sunlight and radiating heat towards the colder sky. The study, titled 'Hierarchically Porous Polymer Coatings for Highly Efficient Passive Daytime Radiative Cooling', was published in journal Science.How coating worksFor PDRC to work effectively, a surface needs to do two things. It must reflect a large amount of sunlight so that it does not gain too much heat, and it must have high thermal emittance so that it can release heat towards the sky.The Columbia Engineering team designed the polymer coating to achieve both. The researchers used a solution-based process known as phase-inversion to create a porous, foam-like structure inside the polymer.The structure contains air voids ranging from the nano to microscale. These tiny spaces help the material scatter and reflect sunlight because air and the surrounding polymer have different refractive indices.This approach also changes how the polymer looks. The polymers used by the researchers can normally be transparent, but the air voids make the material appear white. The researchers therefore used the air voids in place of the pigments normally used to make white paint.The coating has a solar reflectance of more than 96% and a thermal emittance of about 97%. According to the researchers, these properties allowed it to remain significantly cooler than its surroundings under different sky conditions.Air voids replace white pigmentsThe researchers built on earlier work showing that simple polymers such as acrylic, silicone and PET can be effective heat radiators and could be used for PDRC.The main challenge was that these polymers are normally transparent. A transparent material does not reflect enough sunlight for effective daytime radiative cooling. Existing approaches could use reflectors such as silver mirrors, but the researchers wanted a method that would be easier to make and apply.They chose phase-inversion because it is a simple, solution-based method for producing light-scattering air voids inside polymers. Since polymers and solvents are already used in paints, the process could produce a coating that is close to paint in how it can be applied.The researchers said the air voids can reflect sunlight across wavelengths ranging from ultraviolet to infrared. This allows the coating to avoid absorbing much of the incoming solar energy while its thermal properties help it release heat towards the sky.âThis simple but fundamental modification yields exceptional reflectance and emittance that equal or surpass those of state-of-the-art PDRC designs, but with a convenience that is almost paint-like,â lead author Jyotirmoy Mandal said.Impact in desert and tropical conditionsThe researchers tested the material under different environmental conditions to see whether its cooling ability could work beyond a single climate.In the warm, arid desert environment in Arizona, the coating cooled to about 6Â°C below the ambient temperature. In Bangladesh's foggy, tropical environment, it cooled to about 3Â°C below ambient temperature.The difference was important because PDRC can be affected by atmospheric conditions. âThe fact that cooling is achieved in both desert and tropical climates, without any thermal protection or shielding, demonstrates the utility of our design wherever cooling is required,â Yang said.The coating was designed as an exterior material. The researchers said it could be applied to rooftops and buildings, as well as water tanks, vehicles and spacecraft. In principle, it can be used on surfaces that can be painted.The team also worked on color limitation that can affect cooling. Conventional cooling surfaces often rely on white because white materials can reflect sunlight, but exterior surfaces are not always required or preferred to be white.Researchers made coloured versionsThe Columbia team added dyes to create coloured versions of the polymer coating while retaining cooling capabilities. Nanfang Yu said balancing colour and cooling performance was an important part of the work because the colour of an exterior coating can be a matter of choice. He noted that paint manufacturers had been working for years on coloured coatings for uses such as roofs.The researchers also considered environmental and operational factors, including recyclability, biocompatibility and high-temperature operation. Their tests showed that the technique could be applied to different polymers to achieve these properties.Mandal said the wide range of polymers available could allow other properties to be incorporated into PDRC coatings when suitable polymers and solvents are available.Using sky to release heatThe idea behind radiative cooling is that the sky can act as a heat sink. A surface exposed to the sky can lose heat through thermal radiation while reflecting incoming sunlight.Claes-Goran Granqvist, a physics professor at Uppsala University and a pioneer in radiative cooling, who was not involved in the study, said radiative cooling had received less attention from materials scientists than some other methods of heating and cooling.âNature offers many ways for heating and cooling, some of which are extremely well known and widely studied and others that are poorly known,â Granqvist said.He described radiative cooling as one of the less well-known approaches and said the study demonstrated the potential of hierarchically porous polymer coatings.The researchers said their work showed that the coating could provide cooling even in full sunlight. Its porous structure allows sunlight to be reflected, while its thermal emittance allows heat to be radiated towards the sky.Further applicationsAfter demonstrating the cooling effect, Yang, Yu and Mandal continued refining the design for practical use. They also explored the use of completely biocompatible polymers and solvents. The researchers said they were in talks with industry about possible next steps.Yang linked the work to the need for cooling technologies as heat waves and high temperatures affect different parts of the world.âNow is a critical time to develop promising solutions for sustainable humanity,â Yang said. âThis year, we witnessed heat waves and record-breaking temperatures in North America, Europe, Asia, and Australia.âFor Yu, the material also offered an unusual explanation for why the coating appears white. He said he once considered white to be the hardest colour to create in paint. âWhen I studied watercolor painting years ago, white paints were the most expensive,â Yu said.The researchers found that the colour could instead be produced through properly sized air voids inside a transparent material. Yu pointed to examples in nature where air-filled structures create white or silvery appearances.âWe have now demonstrated that white is in fact the most achievable color. It can be made using nothing more than properly sized air voids embedded in a transparent medium,â he said.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Albert Einstein: âIf a cluttered desk is a sign of a cluttered mind, of what, thenâ¦â
articles.summary: Science News: While a desk covered in books, papers and unfinished notes may be seen as a sign of an untidy mind, the great scientist Albert Einstein had a differen.
articles.body: While a desk covered in books, papers and unfinished notes may be seen as a sign of an untidy mind, the great scientist Albert Einstein had a different view of this assumption. In particular, he asked, âIf a cluttered desk is a sign of a cluttered mind, of what, then, is an empty desk a sign?â This statement suggests that the state of a personâs workspace does not always reflect their cognitive abilities. While the work environment of a person may give some clues about their work style, it certainly doesnât reveal all aspects of their thinking. Thus, for some people, a cluttered desk is a working method which implies having all needed references and ideas close at hand. Einsteinâs saying shows that intellectual capacity may be difficult to assess according to oneâs external tidiness.Albert Einstein (1879-1955) was a German theoretical physicist, the author of the theories that have changed the perception of the concepts of space, time, gravity, and the universe. His theory of relativity became one of the cornerstones of modern physics. The description of the photoelectric effect provided by Einstein led to his Nobel Prize in Physics of 1921.Quote of the day by Albert EinsteinâIf a cluttered desk is a sign of a cluttered mind, of what, then, is an empty desk a sign?âWhat does this quote mean?Einstein's question plays with the assumption that external order reflects internal order. If a messy desk automatically meant a messy mind, then we might reasonably expect an empty or perfectly organised desk to indicate an exceptionally clear and productive one. But reality is far more complicated. People have different ways of thinking and working. Some need everything arranged neatly before they can concentrate, while others find that having several books, notes or objects around them helps them make connections between ideas. The important point is that a desk is a workspace, not a window into someone's intelligence.A cluttered desk can sometimes reflect an active mindWhen someone is deeply involved in a project, their surroundings can naturally become crowded. A writer may have several drafts nearby, a scientist may be comparing research papers, and an artist may keep sketches and reference material spread across a table. What appears to be disorder could simply be evidence that the person is actively working through a problem. Of course, excessive clutter can sometimes make work more difficult. But Einstein's point is that we should not automatically assume that every untidy workspace represents confusion. Sometimes, the apparent mess is simply the physical evidence of ideas being developed.An empty desk does not guarantee a clear mindThe humour in Einstein's question comes from applying the same logic in reverse. If we treat a cluttered desk as proof of mental disorder, what should we conclude when a desk contains absolutely nothing? An empty surface could belong to someone highly organised, someone who prefers digital tools, someone who has just finished working or someone who simply has not started yet. The desk itself cannot tell us which explanation is correct. Absence of clutter is not proof of clarity, just as the presence of clutter is not proof of confusion.Creativity does not always follow a neat pathCreative thinking is rarely a perfectly ordered process. One idea can lead to an unexpected question, which can lead to another possibility and eventually change the original direction of a project. Notes may be rewritten, books may be revisited and discarded ideas may suddenly become useful later. This is why creative environments can sometimes look chaotic. The disorder may reflect experimentation rather than a lack of discipline. What matters is whether the person can navigate that environment and turn scattered thoughts into something meaningful.Everyone has a different way of organising their thoughtsThere is no single workspace that works for everyone. One person might prefer an almost completely empty desk, while another might keep everything they need within arm's reach. Some people organise their thoughts visually, surrounding themselves with reminders and notes; others prefer to keep everything stored away until they need it. Neither method is inherently better. Productivity depends less on whether a workspace looks impressive and more on whether it helps the person concentrate, solve problems and make progress.We often judge competence by appearancesThis insight from Einstein is also connected with another tendency which humans possess: that of making snap decisions depending on how things look. For instance, a neat office environment may make one think of a person as organized, while a messy work environment may give one the impression of the opposite. However, things are not always what they seem. The same goes for many other aspects of our lives. A person may be speaking in low tones but have great thoughts in his or her head, may appear calm but work really hard.Sometimes order is useful, but it is not the goalThis does not mean that organisation has no value. A manageable workspace can save time, reduce distractions and make it easier to find important things. For many people, keeping their surroundings organised genuinely improves concentration. But organisation should serve the work rather than become a measure of personal worth. A beautifully arranged desk is useful if it helps someone work better; it is not valuable simply because it looks productive.Einstein's joke carries a serious lessonThe brilliance of the quote lies in how quickly it exposes a weak assumption. We often believe that visible order must reflect mental order, but there is no simple relationship between the two. Einstein's question encourages us to pause before turning an observation into a conclusion. A messy desk tells us that a desk is messy. An empty desk tells us that it is empty. Neither one tells us everything about the person sitting behind it.Why this quote still matters todayIn an era filled with productivity routines, minimalist workspaces and carefully organised digital lives, Einstein's words offer a useful reminder not to confuse appearance with achievement. Organisation can certainly help us work, but intelligence, creativity and curiosity do not have a particular visual style. The lasting lesson behind Einstein's observation is that a productive mind does not have to look organised from the outside. What matters is not whether the desk is perfectly clean or completely covered in papers, but what the person is able to think, discover and create.

articles.title: In 2017, an MIT class project explored a new kind of aircraft; it has now grown into an $850 million Ohio factory plan for an 8-motor hybrid plane that can take off from an area about the length of a soccer field
articles.summary: Science News: A class project at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 2017 studied a new type of aircraft; now, it has ballooned into a $850 million O.
articles.body: A class project at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 2017 studied a new type of aircraft; now, it has ballooned into a $850 million Ohio factory plan for an 8-motor hybrid plane that can take off from an area the size of a soccer field. According to MIT Campus News report, a classroom experiment at MIT could soon change how people view air travel over short distances. As reported, a hybrid aircraft capable of operating without conventional runways is migrating from the university workshop to an intended $850 million manufacturing facility in Ohio, with the potential to enable quieter, faster and more accessible regional flights. The plane is from Electra, a company that grew out of an idea first explored by MIT graduate students in 2017. The end result is an eight-motor hybrid aircraft that can transport nine passengers, travel about 1,200 miles and cruise at around 200 miles per hour.From the MIT classroom to the runwayThe idea was born in the MIT course 16.886 Air Transportation Systems Architecting . SM â19, PhD â24 Chris Courtin was on a student team examining alternatives to the increasingly popular eVTOL concept. The students found that aircraft capable of short takeoffs and landings could be very useful for regional transportation. They wanted to combine light electric motors and batteries with a fixed-wing design, and it eventually became what Electra calls an ultra-short takeoff and landing aircraft. The idea lived on in MIT senior design projects, with students building and testing smaller versions in the Wright Brothers Wind Tunnel and in the air. Courtin later incorporated some of the work into his doctoral research. Aerospace entrepreneur John Langford joined the effort in 2019, and Electra was formally established along with founding technical advisers, MIT professors Mark Drela and John Hansman.Eight engines make up a unique propulsion systemAccording to the news, Electra takes a different approach to hybrid aviation. Instead of a traditional engine operating the propellers, the aircraft has a gas-powered generator in the nose. During takeoff and landing, the generator and two batteries provide power to eight electric motors mounted across the wing. Once the aircraft is at cruising altitude, the generator provides most of the power and recharges the batteries. This arrangement allows the gas engine to be optimized for cruising, not the much higher power requirements of takeoff. The eight motors also produce what is known as a blown-lift effect. This system directs air over the wings to provide sufficient lift to allow the aircraft to operate from areas the length of a soccer field, and that could remove one of the biggest barriers to regional air travel: How to get to an airport in the first place.Airports are not the only destinationElectraâs plane is being designed for trips of roughly 50 to 250 miles, a range that can be a tricky one for both airlines and ground transportation. Instead of several hours of driving to a major airport, passengers may be able to board the aircraft at smaller sites closer to home. The company plans to operate out of places such as parking lots, barges and soccer-field-sized spaces, as long as proper operating permissions and infrastructure are in place. The aircraft could also serve as a shuttle to major airports, allowing travelers to avoid congested roads without a traditional runway at their point of departure. Another potential benefit is noise. Electra says the aircraft can fly more quietly than traditional aircraft and helicopters with many smaller propellers instead of one or two big ones.From prototype to an Ohio plantThe idea is already beyond the drawing board. The two-seat Electra EL2 demonstrator made its first test flights in 2023 and has accumulated more than 200 flights since. The company is now gearing up for its biggest move yet. Electra will spend $850 million to construct a 96-acre manufacturing center in Springfield and Clark County, Ohio. The project is expected to create about 1,975 jobs and construction is expected to start next year. The first stage of the factory should produce up to 400 nine-seater planes per year. A second phase could eventually raise production to about 800 planes a year.Regional flight: A new beginningElectra is also exploring military logistics, cargo transportation and humanitarian uses. But its passenger planes might be the most transformative if the company can make them affordable enough for broad use. This isnât just about building another luxury plane. Electra aims to open regional air travel to many more people, with the simplicity of a fixed-wing plane with electric propulsion assist and ultra-short takeoff capabilities. So, what began as a classroom project at MIT in 2017 is becoming something much bigger: an effort to rethink the airport itself, and maybe make a soccer field as important to the future of regional aviation as a runway.

articles.title: Australia's First Wind Trees Are Spinning and People Are All About It
articles.summary: Two metal trees beside a suburban Perth road are generating electricity every time their leaf-shaped turbines begin to spin. The nine-meter structures are Au...
articles.body:
Two metal trees beside a suburban Perth road are generating electricity every time their leaf-shaped turbines begin to spin.

The nine-meter structures are Australia's first Wind Trees. They stand along Connolly Drive in Clarkson, Western Australia, at the future Catalina Green commercial center.

Each tree carries 36 small wind turbines known as Aeroleaves. Unlike the blades on a conventional wind turbine, the leaves can collect wind coming from any direction and operate independently.

The Catalina Regional Council funded the project, which debuted in December 2025. Electricity from the trees will power lighting around the commercial center.

Embedded media follows. Please allow a moment for it to load.

The individual turbines resemble leaves attached to the branches of a stylized tree. Manufacturer New World Wind says the Aeroleaves begin operating in winds of approximately 8 kilometers per hour.

The direct-drive system does not use belts or gears, which the company says allows it to operate with very little audible noise.

Project supplier EVT Energy estimates that each Catalina tree can produce nearly 5,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity annually. That is enough to power about 15 streetlights or 100 square meters of low-consumption office space.

The two structures are intended to supply car-park lighting at Catalina Green rather than send large amounts of electricity into the wider power grid. More than 200 Wind Trees have been installed across 42 countries, according to the supplier, but the Catalina project is the first Australian installation.

One person wrote on a Facebook Reel about the project, "I have been looking at this wind technology for about 5 years, it was invented in Scandinavia. The beautiful thing is this is much cheaper than wind turbines, and can be put almost anywhere, is much more environmentally friendly, and absolutely a lot less harmful to birds."

Visitors can see them from Connolly Drive

The trees are located at Catalina Estate in Clarkson, one of Perth's northern suburbs. They are visible beside Connolly Drive near the developing Catalina Green commercial precinct.

While they are not necessarily a tourist attraction, people can go check out the trees for free. However, visitors should treat them as public infrastructure and view them from publicly accessible areas without entering the construction site.
